questions.question: Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork under his microscope and saw rows of tiny boxes. In his book Micrographia, in 1665, he named them cells. The cells in cork are dead. What part of each cell was still there for Hooke to see?
questions.context: A plant cell's stiff wall outlasts the living cell inside it. Hooke's cork cells were long dead, so their insides were gone and only the walls were left, holding air; he likened them to the cells of a honeycomb. In a living plant cell, the membrane, the nucleus and the vacuole all sit inside the wall.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade cell units open with Hooke naming cells in cork, and teach that a plant cell has a stiff wall outside its membrane.

questions.question: The first idea of cell theory covers every living thing on Earth, from a bacterium to a person. What does it say every living thing is made of?
choices: Cells that each hold a nucleus
Cells that each have a cell wall
questions.context: Some living things, such as a bacterium, are a single cell, while a person is built of around 30 trillion. A bacterium has no nucleus and a person's cells have no wall, so the only rule that fits every living thing is one or more cells.
questions.grade_note: Cell theory's three ideas are the first thing a 6th-grade cell unit teaches; this is the first, that all living things are made of one or more cells.

questions.question: A boy falls and scrapes his knee, and a scab forms over the wound. Days later, new skin has grown across it beneath the scab. Where did the new skin come from?
questions.answer: Living skin cells at the edge of the wound
choices: Living skin cells at the edge of the wound
Dead skin cells from the skin's outer layer
Dried blood from the scab above it
Clear fluid that seeped out of the wound
questions.context: Cell theory says every new cell comes from a cell that already exists. Living skin cells at the wound's edges multiply and spread across it, while the scab only shields the wound and falls off once the skin has healed. The dead cells of the skin's outer layer can make nothing new.
questions.grade_note: The third idea of cell theory, that new cells come only from cells that already exist, is 6th-grade content; a healing scrape is the everyday case.

questions.question: Biologists sort cells into two great groups. Eukaryotes, such as amoebas and the cells of plants and animals, have a nucleus. Prokaryotes, such as bacteria, have none. A bacterium still carries genetic instructions. Where does it keep them?
questions.context: Every cell carries genetic instructions (DNA). With no nucleus to hold them, a bacterium keeps its DNA in a clump in its cytoplasm, a region called the nucleoid. Bacteria have no mitochondria or chloroplasts at all, and the cell wall is an outer layer, not a store.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade cell units teach the two kinds of cell: prokaryotes such as bacteria, with no nucleus, and eukaryotes, with one.

questions.question: The heart is built of muscle tissue and other kinds of tissue, all working together to pump blood. In the levels of organisation of a living body, what is the heart?
questions.context: A tissue is a group of similar cells doing one job, and an organ is two or more kinds of tissue working together, as in the heart. The heart, the blood vessels and the blood make up the circulatory system, an organ system, and all the body's systems together make the organism.
questions.grade_note: The levels from cell to tissue, organ, organ system and organism are standard 6th-grade content.

questions.question: Every cell has a cell membrane around it, even a plant cell or a bacterium that also has a wall. What job does the membrane do?
questions.answer: It controls what enters and leaves the cell
choices: It controls what enters and leaves the cell
It gives the cell a stiff and boxy shape
It holds the genetic instructions of the cell
It releases the energy stored in the cell's food
questions.context: The membrane is the cell's gatekeeper: it lets in water, oxygen and food and lets out wastes, while keeping the cell's own parts inside. In a plant cell, the stiff wall outside the membrane gives shape and support, but it is the membrane that controls what passes through.
questions.grade_note: The cell membrane's job, controlling what goes in and out, is a core part-and-job fact of the 6th-grade cell unit.

questions.question: A plant or animal cell carries genetic instructions that tell it what to make and how to do its work. Which part of the cell holds those instructions and directs the cell's work?
questions.context: The nucleus is the cell's control centre. It holds the genetic instructions (DNA) and uses them to direct the cell's work, such as making the proteins the cell needs. The cytoplasm is the jelly the cell's parts sit in, and the membrane is the cell's border.
questions.grade_note: That the nucleus holds the cell's genetic instructions and directs its work is a core 6th-grade part-and-job fact.

questions.question: A green cell in a leaf makes its own sugar from sunlight, yet it also holds mitochondria, just as an animal cell does. Why does it need them?
questions.answer: To release the energy stored in that sugar
choices: To release the energy stored in that sugar
To make more sugar at night without sunlight
To store the water that the roots carry up
To let food in and wastes out of the cell
questions.context: Chloroplasts make the sugar, and mitochondria release the energy stored in it, so a leaf cell needs both. Plant and animal cells alike have mitochondria; storing water is the vacuole's job, and the membrane lets things in and out.
questions.grade_note: Mitochondria releasing energy from food is a 6th-grade part-and-job fact, and plant cells having them too corrects a common mix-up.

questions.question: A cell from inside a green leaf can make food from sunlight. A cell scraped from a person's cheek cannot. Which part of the leaf cell does that work?
questions.context: Chloroplasts use light energy, water and carbon dioxide to make sugar, and the green chlorophyll in them gives leaves their colour. Plants and algae have them; animal cells such as cheek cells do not. Mitochondria, which both cells have, release energy from food but make none.
questions.grade_note: That chloroplasts make food from sunlight, in plant cells but not animal cells, is the standard 6th-grade plant-versus-animal-cell fact.

questions.question: A potted plant left without water for a week begins to droop. After a good watering, it stands up straight again. Which part of its cells fills with water and presses outward to hold the plant up?
questions.context: A mature plant cell's large central vacuole stores water and can fill most of the cell. Full, it presses the cell out against its stiff wall and keeps the plant firm; short of water, it shrinks and the plant wilts. Animal cells have smaller, fewer vacuoles.
questions.grade_note: The plant cell's large central vacuole, and the wilting that follows when it runs short of water, are taught in 6th grade with the plant-versus-animal-cell comparison.
